doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

chapter: Oral tradition, teaching and Shiny Stockings
title: Call and response as oral culture
summary: Foster and Hughes discuss jazz as oral tradition, call and response and its male-female conversation.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you something about that and have you just make a comment on this. Can you give us some of your insights, when you talk about head arrangements, with no written music, and people just doing it out of their own experience of knowing the music, somebody starting a riff and the next person automatically knows where that lays on the horn and how to pick that up in unison then how to split it into harmony, or the bari sax automatically knows to play a lower diatone line to that. Can you talk to us about how jazz is a manifestation of oral culture? And a blending of oral culture and literate culture. © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

Well you have to go back to the call and response idea, you know? That’s part of our oral history, right, the call and response. Okay, well in music, in jazz, the trumpets may set one riff, the saxophones will respond by filling in the blank spaces. The trumpets might say [scats] And that’s like a—
But it’s like the two of them are having a conversation.

Like a man and a woman, you know? If the trumpets are playing something up high, and you want to have a response to that on a masculine level, and the trumpets are sounding like the female, then you come in and make your statement behind them to answer like, no you’re not going to do that. And that’s the kind of an attitude you have to have. Like when the trumpets say something, you gotta get in there and get your thing going, you know, and it’s just like he says, the call and response. But to me it’s always been the male/female type thing, you know, the female talks, the male answers, and I don’t know, the reed section kind of mediates the —
